"title": "Mechanochemical synthesis of eco-friendly fertilizer from eggshell (calcite) and KH2PO4",
"authors": "Roger Borges; Amanda Soares Giroto; Rodrigo Klaic; Fernando Wypych; Caue Ribeiro",
"field_subfield": "Materials chemistry / agricultural chemistry (reverse logistics, mechanochemistry, fertilizer science)",
"type_of_paper": "Experimental study (materials synthesis, characterization, and release kinetics)",
"executive_summary": "This study presents an environmentally beneficial and cost-effective method of producing calcium phosphate bioceramics (potassium calcium phosphates) for soil conditioning, based on reverse logistics and green chemistry. The method uses a free-solvent mechanochemical process between eggshell waste (calcite, CaCO3) and monobasic potassium dihydrogen phosphate (KH2PO4). The resulting K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4 phases provide better nutrient management of P, K, and Ca. When applied to soil, the material first releases K and forms hydroxyapatite, serving as an important bioavailable source of P and Ca at pH ~5, which comprises a large part of many countries' soils. Eggshells are important wastes of food industries and excellent CaCO3 sources (more specifically calcite), with everyday millions of tons produced as biowaste around the world, disposed in landfills with no pretreatment and producing odors due to microbial growth. The solid-state mechanochemical activation consists in applying mechanical energy to promote a chemical reaction from solid reagents using mainly friction and impact forces. The process mainly produces K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4, among other non-crystalline compounds and also CO2 resulting from CaCO3 decomposition. Compared to KH2PO4, all these phosphates may exhibit very different solubility according to the different bonds between different metal cations. The produced potassium calcium phosphates may be classified as smart release fertilizers, since they provide a delay of the bioavailability of P and K and also improve the bioavailability of Ca. The solid-state mechanochemical activation allows the reactions to occur in a solvent-free environment, producing no liquid or solid waste in the process. The literature reports the mechanochemical synthesis of hydroxyapatite from different precursors, but no mechanochemical process has been reported for the production of K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4 from calcite provided by eggshell and KH2PO4. The eggshells were collected by the authors in their homes, washed with water and dried at room temperature, presenting a diameter between 1 and 10 mm before the grinding process. The milling process was performed with a high-energy ball mill, Fritsch Pulverisette 7, with a 250 ml zirconia bowl, 5 zirconia balls of 15 mm diameter. The essays were performed using the weight ratio of 1:1 (w/w) of eggshell and KH2PO4 for various times and speeds. After milled, the samples were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD), nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) MAS, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). The nutrient content of the samples and precursors were obtained dissolving the samples by using acid digestion in H2SO4/H2O2 PA mixture (8:1 v/v, by 24 h at 250 °C), and determined by atomic absorption (K and Ca) and colorimetric (P) methods. The phosphorus diffusion rates in soil were performed in Petri dishes containing moist soil, according to the method described by Degryse and Mclaughlin (2014). The kinetic study of the nutrient release was firstly evaluated in citric acid solution (wt 2%) according to the recommended procedure from MAPA. The kinetic study of the nutrient release was also evaluated in soil. The results indicate new phosphate phases such as K3CaH(PO4)2 and KCaPO4, which present in citric acid solution a slower release character of potassium and phosphorus compared to the precursor KH2PO4, and a faster release character compared to the precursor CaCO3 from eggshell. The soil essays performed indicate the same behavior, but a general slower release trend when compared to citric acid solution essays, which can be explained by hydroxyapatite formation. The authors acknowledge support from CNPq, and thank the Agronano Network, the Agroenergy Laboratory, and the National Nanotechnology Laboratory for Agribusiness for providing institutional support and facilities.",

summary.title: Mechanochemical synthesis of eco-friendly fertilizer from eggshell (calcite) and KH2PO4
summary.authors: Roger Borges; Amanda Soares Giroto; Rodrigo Klaic; Fernando Wypych; Caue Ribeiro
summary.field_subfield: Materials chemistry / agricultural chemistry (reverse logistics, mechanochemistry, fertilizer science)
summary.type_of_paper: Experimental study (materials synthesis, characterization, and release kinetics)
summary.executive_summary: This study presents an environmentally beneficial and cost-effective method of producing calcium phosphate bioceramics (potassium calcium phosphates) for soil conditioning, based on reverse logistics and green chemistry. The method uses a free-solvent mechanochemical process between eggshell waste (calcite, CaCO3) and monobasic potassium dihydrogen phosphate (KH2PO4). The resulting K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4 phases provide better nutrient management of P, K, and Ca. When applied to soil, the material first releases K and forms hydroxyapatite, serving as an important bioavailable source of P and Ca at pH ~5, which comprises a large part of many countries' soils. Eggshells are important wastes of food industries and excellent CaCO3 sources (more specifically calcite), with everyday millions of tons produced as biowaste around the world, disposed in landfills with no pretreatment and producing odors due to microbial growth. The solid-state mechanochemical activation consists in applying mechanical energy to promote a chemical reaction from solid reagents using mainly friction and impact forces. The process mainly produces K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4, among other non-crystalline compounds and also CO2 resulting from CaCO3 decomposition. Compared to KH2PO4, all these phosphates may exhibit very different solubility according to the different bonds between different metal cations. The produced potassium calcium phosphates may be classified as smart release fertilizers, since they provide a delay of the bioavailability of P and K and also improve the bioavailability of Ca. The solid-state mechanochemical activation allows the reactions to occur in a solvent-free environment, producing no liquid or solid waste in the process. The literature reports the mechanochemical synthesis of hydroxyapatite from different precursors, but no mechanochemical process has been reported for the production of K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4 from calcite provided by eggshell and KH2PO4. The eggshells were collected by the authors in their homes, washed with water and dried at room temperature, presenting a diameter between 1 and 10 mm before the grinding process. The milling process was performed with a high-energy ball mill, Fritsch Pulverisette 7, with a 250 ml zirconia bowl, 5 zirconia balls of 15 mm diameter. The essays were performed using the weight ratio of 1:1 (w/w) of eggshell and KH2PO4 for various times and speeds. After milled, the samples were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD), nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) MAS, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). The nutrient content of the samples and precursors were obtained dissolving the samples by using acid digestion in H2SO4/H2O2 PA mixture (8:1 v/v, by 24 h at 250 °C), and determined by atomic absorption (K and Ca) and colorimetric (P) methods. The phosphorus diffusion rates in soil were performed in Petri dishes containing moist soil, according to the method described by Degryse and Mclaughlin (2014). The kinetic study of the nutrient release was firstly evaluated in citric acid solution (wt 2%) according to the recommended procedure from MAPA. The kinetic study of the nutrient release was also evaluated in soil. The results indicate new phosphate phases such as K3CaH(PO4)2 and KCaPO4, which present in citric acid solution a slower release character of potassium and phosphorus compared to the precursor KH2PO4, and a faster release character compared to the precursor CaCO3 from eggshell. The soil essays performed indicate the same behavior, but a general slower release trend when compared to citric acid solution essays, which can be explained by hydroxyapatite formation. The authors acknowledge support from CNPq, and thank the Agronano Network, the Agroenergy Laboratory, and the National Nanotechnology Laboratory for Agribusiness for providing institutional support and facilities.

claims.description: A free-solvent mechanochemical process between eggshell waste and KH2PO4 can produce new potassium calcium phosphate phases that improve nutrient management of P, K, and Ca in soil.
The new phosphates phases from milling made calcium readily available, an opposite effect to the delay observed for phosphorus and potassium.

The results indicate new phosphate phases such as K3CaH(PO4)2 and KCaPO4, which present in citric acid solution a slower release character of potassium and phosphorus compared to the precursor KH2PO4, and a faster release character compared to the precursor CaCO3 from eggshell. The soil essays performed indicate the same behavior, but a general slower release trend when compared to citric acid solution essays, which can be explained by hydroxyapatite formation. Research Context
Reverse logistics is an instrument of economic and social development characterized by a set of actions, procedures and means to enable the collection and restitution of solid waste to the business sector, for reuse, in its cycle or in other cycles productive, or other environmentally appropriate final destination. An application of this concept is to provide novel processes for the synthesis of different calcium and / or potassium phosphates from any source of calcium carbonate (CaCO3), making it a soil conditioner. Among sources, eggshells are important wastes of food industries and excellent CaCO3 sources (more specifically calcite) (Byeon, 2016), with monobasic potassium dihydrogen phosphate. Everyday millions of tons of eggshells are produced as biowaste around the world, disposed in landfills with no pretreatment and producing odors due to microbial growth. Normally the reactions are processed by solid state mechanochemical activation, to produce different materials concerning physico-chemical features, especially the solubilization and diffusion of its constitutional elements and chemical species. Basically, the solid-state mechanochemical activation consists in applying mechanical energy to promote a chemical reaction (Kouznetsov et al., 2016) from solid reagents using mainly friction and impact forces. The process mechanism involved is still quite complex to evaluate, but the applied energy must be large enough to be able to break the reagent bonds and promote solid phase ion migration, in the case of this study, to form a new structure. The literature reports the mechanochemical synthesis of hydroxyapatite (Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2) from different precursors to those reported in this study (Chaikina et al., 2019), and even if from eggshell, the method uses phosphoric acid solution instead of powder phosphate salts (Francis and Rahman, 2016). Thus, as far as the authors know, no mechanochemical process has been reported for the production of calcium and potassium hydrogen phosphate (K3CaH(PO4)2) and potassium calcium phosphate (CaKPO4) from calcite provided by eggshell and KH2PO4, i.e. different structures from hydroxyapatite including potassium as one of the main components. It is in this sense that new technologies of ecological fertilizer production have been prioritizing environmental care using industrial and other potential wastes in the formulation of new products (Ivanov et al., 2019; Krishna et al., 2017; Santos et al., 2019; Cichy et al., 2019), avoiding unnecessary economic losses, are primarily relevant in the current socio-environmental scenario.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a free-solvent mechanochemical process between eggshell waste and KH2PO4 can produce new potassium calcium phosphate phases that improve nutrient management of P, K, and Ca in soil. The study hypothesizes that the produced potassium calcium phosphates may be classified as smart release fertilizers, since they provide a delay of the bioavailability of P and K and also improve the bioavailability of Ca. The study hypothesizes that these materials would promote better nutrient management by delaying the bioavailability of phosphorus and potassium (which are highly soluble from KH2PO4) and increasing the calcium bioavailability. The study hypothesizes that the new phosphates phases from milling made calcium readily available, an opposite effect to the delay observed for phosphorus and potassium. The study hypothesizes that the slower release for calcium and phosphorus for 2 h/600 rpm sample and the P radial diffusion are probably related to hydroxyapatite formation, identified from 3 until 30 days in soil conditions. The predicted outcome is that the material first releases K and forms hydroxyapatite, serving as an important bioavailable source of P and Ca at pH ~5, which comprises a large part of many countries' soils. The predicted outcome is that these materials would exhibit very different solubility according to the different bonds between different metal cations, influenced by the size of the metal cation and its charge, influencing the reticular energy of the structure.

Methodological Details
The eggshells were collected by the authors in their homes, washed with water and dried at room temperature, presenting a diameter between 1 and 10 mm before the grinding process. The KH2PO4 PA was supplied from Vetec. The milling process was performed with high-energy ball mill, Fritsch Pulverisette 7, with a 250 ml zirconia bowl, 5 zirconia balls of 15 mm diameter. The essays were performed using the weight ratio of 1:1 (w/w) of eggshell and KH2PO4 were performed firstly for 15 min, 30 min, 1 h, 2 h, 3 h, 6 h, 12 h and 24 h at 600 rpm, and secondly at 100, 200, 400 and 600 rpm for 2 h. Considering the purity of KH2PO4 and assuming that the eggshells are mainly composed by CaCO3, the mixture corresponds to 0.75 mmol of KH2PO4 and 1 mmol of CaCO3. After milled, the samples were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD), nuclear magnetic resonance, magic-angle spinning (NMR) MAS, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). The nutrient content of the samples and precursors were obtained dissolving the samples by using acid digestion in H2SO4/H2O2 PA mixture (8:1 v/v, by 24 h at 250 °C), and determined by atomic absorption (K and Ca) and colorimetric (P) methods. Before release essays at citric acid solution (2 wt%), the material has been pelletized to simulated commercial products. The pellets were obtained in steel pelletizer applying the pressure of 5 bar, and the weight was standardized to 100 mg/L of P. One single pellet were used in each essay in triplicate, that was placed in 10 mL beaker, this small beaker was immersed into 300 mL of 2% citric acid solution in a 600 mL beaker, the system was kept closed with polyvinyl chloride (PVC) film, in a constant temperature room at 25 °C and under a magnetic stirring. The stirring ensures homogeneous distribution of diffused elements, and aliquots of 1.2 mL at different times (from 15 min to 30 days) have been collected to evaluate the release behavior and allow the calculation of a release kinetic model of Ca, K and P. The phosphorus diffusion rates in soil were performed in Petri dishes containing moist soil, according to the method described by Degryse and Mclaughlin (2014).

Procedures And Architectures
This method consists to use a pre-treated paper to mark the P diffusion in soil. In each Petri dish with diameter of 8.6 cm, 78 g of dry and sieved 2.0 mm mesh soil were added to achieve the desired density of 1.2 g.cm -3. In order to achieve 70% of the maximum soil water retention capacity, 15 mL deionized water were added. The papers are scanned and analyzed using image software (GNU Image Manipulation Program, v. 2.6.11, Free Software). The scanned images are converted to black-with binary images, using a threshold color value (e.g. on a 0-255 scale), and the area of the high P-zone is quantified using the histogram command. In order to investigate the release behavior closer to real conditions, soil release essays were carried out under aerobic conditions in plastic container containing 50 g of sandy soil (Table S2) with 75% water saturation. The experiments were performed at 3, 7, 15 and 30 days, using a single pellet for each container, the pellet weight was standardized to 300 mg of P per kg of soil. After each release period the solid residues samples were removed from the soil and characterized by XRD; potassium and calcium were extracted from the soil by HCl (0.05 Mol/L) and KCl (1 Mol/L) methods, respectively; and phosphorus was extracted from soil using Mehlich 1 method (Embrapa, 1979). A colorimetric analyses of molybdenum blue was used to quantify phosphorus released content into the solution (Murphy and Riley, 1962) and potassium and calcium released content were quantify by flame atomic absorption spectroscopy (FAAS), with a PerkinElmer PinAAcle 900T instrument, in flame atomization mode. The XRD patterns of the powders obtained after milling are shown in Fig. 1. The milling process between KH2PO4 and eggshell (98% of CaCO3) performed from 2 h and 400 rpm produce a mixture of phosphates, mainly K3CaH(PO4)2 (PDF database n° 22-1218 indicated by black columns, and black dash lines guiding the comparison with the samples) and possibly CaKPO4 (PDF database n° 33-1002 indicated by red columns, and red dash lines guiding the comparison with the samples). Bellow these milling parameters (time and milling speed) only the reactants diffraction patterns are found, i.e., no evidence of chemical reaction is observed.

Key Results
The milling process between KH2PO4 and eggshell (98% of CaCO3) performed from 2 h and 400 rpm produce a mixture of phosphates, mainly K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4. There is a direct relationship between the time and milling speed and the increasing of total energy involved. In general, it was noticed that only a minimal energy is required to initiate the mechanochemical reaction and, as a consequence, the diffraction patterns have huge changes attributed to the formation of different polymorphic potassium calcium phosphate phases. The TGA curve of KH2PO4 show two main loss events: since it is an anhydrous material, the moisture loss is not seen and the first step at 200°C should be associated to crystallization water loss. The second step at 300°C corresponds to polycondensation, concomitant with structural water loss. The residual mass (89%) regards to KPO3 formation is consistent to the theoretical (87%) (Fig. 2). The thermal degradation of eggshell has two main steps: a first mass loss step below 300 °C attributed to moisture elimination concomitant with organic membrane degradation; and a second step related to calcite decomposition below 700 °C. The eggshells are mainly composed by CaCO3, as attested by XRD pattern (Fig. 1), which is also confirmed by the small difference from experimental residue (56%) and the theoretical (59%). In the case of milled samples (Fig. 2), three mass loss events are observed: the first step, centered at 280°C, is related to crystallization water loss concomitant with physically adsorbed moisture elimination. The second step, centered at 420°C, is associated to partial structural water loss and structure dimerization, and the final step, centered at 710°C corresponds to final structural water loss reaction and structure polycondensation. It suggests that in low rotation speeds do not provide enough energy to degrade the total amount of calcite to form calcium potassium phosphates. In all cases, a similar thermal behavior related to crystalline phases formation was identified -except for milling during 2 h at 600 rpm, this sample has an unclear phosphate phase, but after thermal treatment at 280 °C it slightly changes matching with K3CaH(PO4)2 phase.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results indicate that the phosphates obtained by milling improve the nutrients management maintaining their bioavailability. For both nutrients there was a substantial decrease of the kinetic constant from KH2PO4 to milled samples, attesting the delay in nutrient supply after mechanochemical processing and certainly related to the formation of potassium calcium phosphate phases (K3CaH(PO4)2 and KCaPO4). But, phosphorus and potassium presented better correlation with pseudo-second order model, considering 'R 2 ' and the values related to concentration at equilibrium time 'qe' and 'experimental qe' (Table 1). It is important to highlight that in this case was observed an opposite effect: the new phosphates phases from milling made calcium readily available. These results indicate that sample 2 h/600 rpm presented a longer delay in phosphorus release compared to the precursor (KH2PO4), corroborating with the results observed in citric acid solution. In summary, results showed that the P radial diffusion profile from sample milled for 2h/600 rpm is intermediate, 34% faster than struvite and 22% slower than precursor at the end of 30 days. There is no increase in the bioavailable calcium when eggshell precursor (CaCO3) is applied in soil, but this concentration increases to 30.97 mg/kg after 30 days for 2 h/600 rpm sample, corresponding to around 8% of calcium recovery from sample (Fig. 6). The slower release for calcium and phosphorus for 2 h/600 rpm sample and the P radial diffusion are probably related to hydroxyapatite formation -(Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2) (PDF database n° 9-432 indicated by green columns) -identified from 3 until 30 days in soil conditions (Fig. 7).

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the free-solvent mechanochemical process between eggshell waste and KH2PO4 to produce new potassium calcium phosphate phases that improve nutrient management of P, K, and Ca in soil. 2. The strongest evidence is that the P radial diffusion profile from sample milled for 2h/600 rpm is intermediate, 34% faster than struvite and 22% slower than precursor at the end of 30 days. 3. The future path is the use of sample 2h/600rpm as nanocomposites to promote better solubilization of P and Ca, as verified in the work of Giroto et al. (2017).
